Question: Why does Indian Railways still use diesel locos in electrified sections? For some minimum non-electrified sections, the whole route is hauled by diesel loco motives.
Answer: This is probably the most genuine question a rail enthusiast or curious person will ask. Recently, few trains in the North Eastern and Northern Railways got diesel links instead of their regular e-locos. This made us curious, as normally trains get an e-loco as an upgrade, but in this case, a train was getting a diesel loco from an e-loco that had HOG technology. Now railways were burning double fuel: to run locomotives and to run generator cars for supplies. After a small study, I found a reason for this case: Railways have been continuously electrifying routes and assigning e-locos to the trains, due to which hundreds of diesel locos are standing in the shed. To keep them fit for running, Railway came up with this concept. It started assigning diesel locomotives to a few trains for a while so that they are always fit to run in emergency situations. The second most common reason is availability. For semi-electrified sections, it is very important to keep a sufficient number of locos at the point where traction is changing, which is possible at big stations only, as you will require a large staff to handle this, and they need a place to stay, food, and other basic facilities. In the case of fully electrified sections, availability is again an issue. There are chances when e-locos are not available or found unfit to run at the last moment. In that case, whatever loco is available will be assigned to that train, and that is why you can also find some freight locos hauling express trains. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️. Thank you for your valuable time.

Question: Why do electric trains show a jerky start, unlike the smooth-start of diesel-powered trains earlier in India? Is it not supposed to be smoother?
Answer: This problem is occurring with LHB coaches hauled by WAP-7 specifically. Last year, I was travelling from Kanyakumari to Dibrugarh by Vivek Express and then from Dibrugarh to Lucknow by Dibrugarh Rajdhani. Both the trains were hauled by WAP-7 locomotives. Regular jerks for almost 7 days annoyed me a lot, and it made me curious to know more about this problem and its cause. Later, I found two possible reasons: 1. The WAP-7 is a modified locomotive. A WAG-9 locomotive was modified for a passenger train locomotive in which the gear ratio was changed, and this might be a reason that the gear ratio is causing some sort of jerk before picking up. 2. The experience of Locopilot is also an important factor. A friend of mine who is a locopilot said that the experience of a locopilot matters in this case. If locopilot applies more power than required, the train suddenly picks up with a jerk. However, both the reasons are based on my own observation and talks with a few loco pilots. One important point to notice is that the LHB coaches have no buffers (stoppers) between two coaches, which we can find in ICF coaches. They act as jerk absorbers. We might be noticing even small jerks in the absence of these buffers. However, if you know the exact reason behind these jerks, do share it with us in the comment section. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️. Question: What should the public bear a part of the cost of travel of passengers in the Vande Bharat luxury train? As per Railway only 57% of the cost is recovered from the passengers.
Answer: 57% of the cost recovered by Railways is no longer true. Trainsets like the Vande Bharat Express are very efficient for the railways. Such trains generate profit even if they run at 50% of their occupancy. Let’s calculate the amount spent by the Railways in operating Vande Bharat Express trains and earned from the passengers. The engine power of the Vande Bharat Express with all its motors is 9000 horsepower( 6750 KW) approx. Disclaimer: 6750 units per hour are consumed if the train operates at full power from start to finish, which is, not possible or necessary during the journey. Power consumed will differ as the train moves through its journey, consuming more power at the start and using less when it's already in motion Here,we are calculating for Varanasi Vande Bharat Express. It consumes 6750 units in 1 hour, which will be 6750×8 = 54000 units. Here, 8 is the number of hours Varanasi Vande Bharat takes to reach Varanasi from New Delhi. Indian Railways gets electricity at a cost of Rs 3.7–7 per unit (depending on the supplier). We are taking Rs. 4.5 per unit, which will cost 54000 × 4.5 = Rs. 2,43,000. We are taking Rs. 22,000 as salary for locopilots, train managers, and other technical staff. We are not taking the catering charges; hence, the amount will be removed from the fare as well. On adding up Rs. 2,43,000 + 22,000 We get Rs. 2,65,000 as the operational cost of Varanasi Vande Bharat for a single run. Now, let’s calculate the revenue collected from the fare. Varanasi Vande Bharat runs with 16 coaches, of whom 14 are chair car coaches and 2 are executive coaches. The total capacity of the train is 1126 seats, including 104 seats of executive class. Fare from New Delhi to Varanasi for Chair car is Rs 1441 (excluding catering charges). Executive class is Rs 2936 (excluding catering charges). The train mostly runs at 100% occupancy, but considering some partially booked seats, we are taking 80% occupancy for both classes. 80% of 1022 is 817 seats. 80% of 104 is 83 seats. Now calculating the final revenue 817×1441 + 83×2936= Rs. 14,20,985 is the estimated amount that the railway gets as revenue from the Varanasi Vande Bharat passengers. If we calculate the profit, 14,20,985 - 2,65,000 We get a profit of Rs. 11,55,985/run. Now, you might have got that the Railways is no longer taking just 57% of the passengers' costs; it is earning well. However, there are many other factors like infrastructure, maintainance & manufactoring cost which I have not included in this calculation as the purpose was just to give an idea about the revenue and the operational cost. This was only one case; if we talk about the current scenario, then there are very few trains remaining that are running at a loss; otherwise, after electrification, most of the trains are profitable. In case you are curious to know then the manufactoring cost of one such train can be recovered in 16 months of operation with above mentioned profit. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️ Thank you for your valuable time.

Question: Can we catch the Vande Bharat train at Varanasi railway station if our reservation is from Prayagraj railway station to Delhi?
Answer: Catching a train one station before the actual boarding point is one of the frequently asked questions on Quora. If we talk about the rule book, then a passenger is allowed to board the train from its boarding station only. In some cases, people book the ticket from station A to station D and set station B as a boarding station. Days later, they decide to board the train only from station A since their ticket is booked from station A, but that is not allowed as well. No matter from where you have booked your ticket, you can only board the train at your boarding station. Now what if you boarded the mail/express train or a premium train, like the Vande Bharat Express, one station before your boarding point? Question: What does the CRS report say about the Odisha train accident? Who is accountable for it?
Answer: A much-awaited CRS report has been handed over to the Ministry of Railways this Wednesday, in which two departments, i.e., Signalling & Telecom staff and Operations staff, were accountable for the decade's biggest accident, where 288 innocent passengers lost their lives and hundreds of them got injured. The accident happened on June 2 this year, when a fast-moving coromondel express suddenly entered a loop line at Bahanaga Bazar in Odisha and hit a freight train loaded with iron ore. The impact of this accident was huge, as the last three coaches of Coromondel exp jumped and hit the last two coaches of another train passing through the down line named SMVT-HWH exp. Let me tell you that the Coromondel Express had received a green signal to run through the Bahanaga Bazar railway station, where the Locopilots were driving the train at the maximum permissible speed of 130 kmph. Due to a failure in track switch No. 17 A, the route got set for a loop line, which can handle a speed of just 40–50 kmph. High speed resulted in a sudden derailment, and the freight ahead caused a lot of damage. For more details, you can read my previous answer, where I have explained things in detail. In the CRS report, It has been found that the signalling maintainer submitted a “disconnection memo” to the station master to carry out repair work, as is the due process. After the work was done, a “reconnection memo” was also issued, meaning that the electronic interlocking signalling system was live. But the safety protocol of testing the signalling system before allowing a train to pass was not followed. Moreover, the signalling staff continued to attend to the work even after the reconnection memo was issued, adding that the responsibility for the accident therefore fell jointly on the station’s operations staff as well as the signalling maintenance staff. The report also found lapses in the protocols in vogue to access the relay room, which is the nerve centre of the electronic interlocking signalling system for which both the signalling staff and the station master are accountable in the railway system. It is the protocol that whenever maintenance of assets of any nature is carried out, the operations staff is also responsible for the safety of trains along with the engineering staff concerned, be it track-related or signalling-related. Days later, the Railway Board transferred Kharagpur Divisional Railway Manager (DRM) Shujat Hashmi and the South Eastern Railway heads of the departments of signalling, Safety, Security, and commercial. On Friday, South Eastern Railway General Manager Archana Joshi was transferred as General Manager of the Rail Wheel Plant, Bengaluru. The Additional General Manager of North Eastern Railway, A. K. Mishra, was appointed the new GM of South Eastern Railway. The Ministry of Railways is going through the report, and let's see what steps they take after reading it. Such negligence is not acceptable at any cost, as it results in the loss of hundreds of innocent lives. Question: Why did my confirmed ticket in the 3rd AC get changed in 3E after the chart was prepared?
Answer: This has been a regular practise of the Indian Railways for almost 3 months and will continue until mid-July. But the question is: why are railways doing that? The story begins in 2020, when Indian Railways decided to introduce a new class in order to provide an alternate option for non-AC sleeper class passengers. It was promoted as an upgrade for non-ac sleeper class passengers as it was going to be an air-conditioned class named 3 AC Economy, and the fare was planned to keep as close as possible to the non-ac sleeper class fare, but The class 3E was launched with a fare close to AC 3 tier which was almost double the fare of sleeper class coaches, which cannot be considered an alternative for non-AC class passengers. In order to make the coach efficient, the railway reduced the dimensions of all the berths and increased the number of berths from 72 to 84. They also removed the storage space for linen, which resulted in a blocked gate as bundles are kept there. Overall, it was a very uncomfortable experience for a passenger travelling in a 3AC Economy coach. In fact, the fare difference between 3 AC and 3E was just 100 for a distance of 1400 km, which is not so fascinating for someone who can afford 3 AC. This all resulted in negative feedback from the passengers, and ultimately, the railways decided to reverse their decision and run these coaches separately as special trains. It released an order for the removal of 3E coaches from the trains in November last year. After 4 months, on March 21, 2023, the railways suddenly issued a circular and restored all the 3E coaches with immediate effect. This time, Railways was not in the mood to take feedback or something. It had a clear intention of forcing us to travel in 3E coaches. Since the advance booking period is 120 days, the reservations were already done until mid-July at the time the circular was issued, so the railway came up with the idea of downgrading the tickets. For example: If a train had 9 3AC coaches and post-circular 2 3AC coaches were replaced with 3E, all the passengers of B8 and B9 would be downgraded to 3E at the time of charting. The fare difference will be credited to their original source of payment. Counter ticket holders are supposed to receive the amount at ticket booking counters. Basically, Railways is forcing us to travel in 3AC Economy coaches by taking such steps as 3E are more profitable than a 3AC coach. I was shocked when the railways removed all the 3AC coaches from a very popular train named 12533 Pushpak SF Express and replaced them with 3E coaches. Question: How do the Indian railways decide which track to allocate to which train?
Answer: After the Odisha train accident, almost everyone had a few questions in their minds. This is one of them: how do Indian Railways decide which track to allocate to which train? In this answer, we will try to understand the procedure, which includes the allocation of tracks. There are various categories of railway stations in India, starting from 2 tracks to as many as 20–30 tracks. We will discuss this in two categories: i) Stations having two tracks (one main line and one loop line) ii) Stations having more than two tracks( one or two main lines and multiple loop lines) Before explaining these points, let me quickly describe the main line and the loop line. Main Line: A line that is built for high speed and uninterrupted operation of trains. In this line, trains generally run at the maximum permissible speed. Loop line: A loop line is built at the railway stations to handle the stoppage of trains so that the main line remains clear for trains that are supposed to skip the station. A loop line can handle a limited speed of 30–50 kmph, which is generally much lower than the speed of a main line. Now, let's get back to our question: In any type of station, the station master, under the guidance of the section controller, sets the route of a train passing through his or her station. In the case of i) Stations having two tracks (one main line and one loop line): The majority of the trains run through the main line, but if a train has to stop, cross, or has to be overtaken, it will go on the loop line so that the main line is kept clear for the other train. However, this is not a fixed procedure, as it depends on the situation. Overall, the station master, under the guidance of the section controller, allocates the track to any train. There are mainly 3–4 scenarios, like stoppage, crossing, overtaking, etc., under which a decision is taken. ii) Stations having more than two tracks( one or two main lines and multiple loop lines): Along with the scenarios mentioned in the first point, there are many other scenarios under which a track allocation is done in the case of many tracks on a railway station. For example, 1. If it is a premium train, then there is a high possibility that its track will be set at either PF 1 or 2 to facilitate the passengers. 2. If it is a junction station, then the track will be allocated according to the side to which a train is supposed to go. If a train has to turn left on a new route after the station, then a track that is easily connected to that route will be allocated to the train. 3. In a general scenario, the availability of the platform is also taken into consideration before allocating the track 4. Some trains have a fixed platform, so in that case, a station authority tries to allocate the same platform. They might change if the platform is occupied by another train. These are some common scenarios under which a station master, following the instructions from a section controller, allocates the track to any train. The section controller is the one who decides which has to go or which has to stop. A station master cannot do this on his own. I hope the procedure for allocating the track is clear now. If you have any further questions, let me know in the comment section. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️. Thank you for your valuable time.

Question: How did the trains collide in the Odisha accident?
Answer: It was a human error. Yes, as per the latest reports, the Odisha train accident, which was a disaster, happened because of human error. You might have read many answers on Quora and seen many videos on YouTube where people are cursing the anti-collision device, but the actual reason is that the track switch that sets the path of the train failed because of a human error. Let me quickly summarise the scenario first. On Friday evening, the Coromondel Express bound for Chennai was heading towards its next stop, Bhadrakh. The train was supposed to skip the Bahanga Bazar railway station and travel through the main line at its maximum permissible speed, which is 130 kmph. On duty, the Assistant Station Master of Bahanga Bazar set the route and gave the proceed signal to the approaching coromondal exp. At the same time, another train that was heading towards Howrah got the green signal on the down line for a skip to Bahanga Bazar. The SMVT-HWH exp. entered Bahanga Bazar first and skipped 80% of the station when it met the Coromondal exp., which was coming on the up line. The signal for Coromondel exp was green, as the train was supposed to skip the station through the main line, but due to the failure of track switch no. 17 A, the route for Coromondal exp got set for loop line. Now let me tell you that the speed to enter a loop line is set between 30 and 50 kmph, which is almost three times lower than the speed of the main line. Locopilots were following the signal instructions, and they entered the yard at the maximum permissible speed. As soon as the train touched the point switch, which was set for the loop line, it got derailed because of the high speed, and the train ran over a freight train that was waiting on the loop line for its signal. This was a horrible accident, but it turned even worse when the last 3 coaches of the Coromandel Express jumped and hit the other train (the Smvt-Hwh Express), which was passing through the down line Two coaches from SMVT-HWH Exp. also got derailed. The last three coaches of Coromondel Exp. and the last two coaches of SMVT-HWH Exp. were general unreserved coaches, which resulted in more injuries and deaths as they were completely packed. Now, let's discuss why the track switch failed. As per the reports, there was maintenance work going on in the section, and the same point, i.e., 17 A, was maintained by the Signalling & Telecom staff a few hours ago. They made a mistake while setting up the relays at that point. The path for Coromondel Express was commanded to be set on the main line, but it didn't happen, and the path remained set for the loop line. It was a failure in the mechanism due to which the signal received incorrect information and turned green for Coromondel Exp. A high-level investigation is going on to find out the exact reasons and who is responsible for this accident. At this stage, signalling and telecom staff seem accountable for this accident. Question: Why do some train stations have only one passenger platform but has 2 railways? How does a train from the opposite side go to the other?
Answer: India, being a massive country, has one of the largest railway networks in the world, which operates close to 28000 trains (passenger and freight) daily. There are almost 7400 railway stations in the Indian railway network to manage the smooth operations of the Indian Railways. The purpose of developing a railway station is not only to provide a platform for passengers but also to manage the massive traffic on Indian tracks. If we observe the network, we can find a railway station after every 4–8 km, and there is a reason behind that. Not all stations are purposely opened for passengers; some do not have a lot of foot fall, but they are very important for the railways. But why? So, the purpose of building a railway station after every 4–8 km and developing at least 2 railway tracks is to manage train operations properly. A second track is helpful in: i) Crossing: If two trains are supposed to cross each other, this scenario is common and useful on sections with single tracks. In that case, trains can only cross each other at these railway stations. Developing a raikway station after every 4–8 km helps in reducing the wait time for each train. ii) Overtake: If one train has to overtake the other train, in such senarios, railway stations play an important role in both single-line and double-line sections. iii) For idle rakes: Sometimes we find an empty rake at Railway Statiins. Generally, they are idled at slightly bigger stations so that the station is able to keep at least 2 tracks free for operations, but if necessary, small stations with 2 tracks use the loop line (second track) for idle rakes. iv) In case of technical failures or accidents: The second track always helps in these scenarios to park such trains and keep the main line clear for other trains. These were a few major benefits of having at least one extra track at railway stations. Mostly there is no second platform at railway stations is because of low footfall at that particular station, and in such cases, platform no. 1 is used for passenger trains so that people can easily board or deboard. Building a plstform and keeping operational requires a decent amount of money which railway avoids to spend if the foot fall at that railway station is low but a second track is important for the reasons I mentioned above. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️. Question: How does Indian Railways decide the route and timetables for new trains?
Answer: We often think about this question whenever a new train launches. Today I will share a detailed explanation of how Indian Railways decides the route and timetable of a new train. The Indian Railways follows a comprehensive process to decide the route and timetables for new trains. The following steps are involved in this process: 1. Traffic Survey: The first step in deciding the route and timetable for a new train is conducting a traffic survey. During this survey, Indian Railways analyzes the demand for a new train and its feasibility in terms of passenger and freight traffic. The survey also takes into account the competition from other modes of transportation. 2. Feasibility Study: Based on the data collected during the traffic survey, Indian Railways carries out a feasibility study to determine the viability of the proposed train. This study includes an analysis of the infrastructure required for the train, the availability of resources such as locomotives and coaches, and the potential revenue that the train could generate. 3. Route Planning: Once the feasibility study is complete, Indian Railways decides on the route for the new train. This involves selecting the origin and destination stations, as well as the intermediate stations that the train will stop at. The route is chosen based on the demand for the train, the availability of infrastructure, and the competition from other modes of transportation. 4. Timetable Planning: After the route has been finalized, Indian Railways prepares a timetable for the new train. The timetable includes the departure and arrival times for each station along the route, as well as the duration of the journey. The timetable is designed to ensure that the train operates efficiently and maximizes passenger and freight traffic. 5. Approval Process: Once the route and timetable have been finalized, the proposal for the new train is submitted for approval. The proposal is reviewed by various departments within Indian Railways, such as the Commercial, Traffic, and Mechanical departments, before it is approved. 6. Implementation: After the proposal has been approved, Indian Railways proceeds with the implementation of the new train. This involves arranging for the necessary resources such as locomotives and coaches, as well as coordinating with other departments to ensure that the train operates smoothly. Overall, the process of deciding the route and timetables for new trains in Indian Railways is a detailed and comprehensive process that involves multiple steps and departments. The aim is to ensure that the train is viable, efficient, and meets the needs of the passengers and the organization. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️. Question: Does a bogie in a train mean the same as a coach or is it different?
Answer: Both are different. In the context of Indian Railways, "bogie" and "coach" are often used interchangeably, but there is a slight difference between the two. A "bogie" refers to the wheeled undercarriage that supports a train's cars or coaches. Each bogie typically has two or more axles with wheels attached to a frame that connects to the car or coach. A "coach" is the passenger-carrying car that is attached to the bogie. A coach can have several bogies attached to it, depending on its length and weight. Each coach typically has seats or berths for passengers, as well as amenities such as toilets, air conditioning, fans and lights. So in summary, a bogie is the wheeled undercarriage that supports a coach, while a coach is the passenger-carrying car that is attached to the bogie. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️. Question: What innovations are making railways the safest mode of transport?
Answer: I won’t say the safest but definitely the following innovations/steps have made the Indian Railways a much safer mode of transportation over the years:- 1. Train Protection and Warning System (TPWS): This is an advanced train protection system that helps to prevent accidents caused by the signal overshooting, excessive speed or driver error. 2. Anti-Collision Device (ACD): This is a radio-based device that helps to avoid collisions between trains. It sends out an alarm to the drivers of the trains in case they are on a collision course. It’s advanced version is KAVACH which protects from head to head collisions. It stops both the trains well ahead if they are suppose to collide each other. Head to head collisions are destructive which we all saw in Gaisal train accident. This technology was recently launched hence the installation is still under process. As of March, 2023, Kavach has been installed over 3000 kms of route. 3. Fog Safety Device: This is a GPS-based system that helps the driver to know the exact location of the train in dense fog. It also warns the driver if the train is about to cross a signal or a level crossing. 4. Electronic Interlocking System: This is a computer-based system that controls the movements of trains at railway stations. It helps to prevent collisions between trains by ensuring that only one train occupies a particular track section at a time. 5. Automatic Fire and Smoke Detection System: This system is installed in the coaches to detect the presence of fire or smoke. It triggers an alarm in the driver's cabin and also activates the fire extinguishing system. 6. CCTV Surveillance: Indian Railways have installed CCTV cameras at stations and in coaches to monitor the movements of passengers and identify any suspicious activities. 7. Mobile Applications: Indian Railways have developed mobile applications like RailSaathi and UTS for the safety of passengers. RailSaathi provides emergency medical assistance, while UTS helps to avoid the rush at railway stations by enabling passengers to book tickets in advance. 8. Introduction of LHB coaches: One of the most important adoption of Indian railways in last 2–3 decades is LHB coaches. Traditional ICF coaches were not safe at all especially in case of high speed derailments. ICF coaches use to climb their succissor coaches and cause a lot of damage to the property and lives but LHB coaches are much more safer. They are designed in a way that theey never climb over other coaches hence they don’t cause heavy damages. 9. Removal of Level crossings: Level crossings are not only dangerous for vehicles but also for the trains in case of high speed collisions. Such accidents do result into a heavy damage to the locomotives and in some case derailments do happen.Removing a lot of level crossings and making under passes has definitely reduced the accidents at the level crossings. 10. Installation of automatic doors: Another much-appreciated step taken by the railways is the shift toward automatic doors. A closed door ensures more safety for the passengers and reduces the risk of falling down and theft. Apart from above mentioned innovations/steps, Indian railways is also working on few innovations like 1. Broken Rail Detection System 2. Rail Stress Monitoring System 3. Headway Improvement System for suburban section 4. Automation of Track Inspection Activities 5. Development of analytical tool by using digital data for improving passenger services 6. Track Cleaning Machine App for post-training revision and self-service refresher courses 7. Use of Remote Sensing, Geomatics and GIS for bridge inspection These are some of the innovations that Indian Railways have implemented over last two decades with an intention of making railways a much safer mode of transportation. Question: Why does the railway allow to book waitlist tickets more even though they’re not allotting confirmed tickets? Is it to earn money?
Answer: There are certain cases where you might feel that the railways is trying to earn money from waitlisted tickets, but the actual reason for allowing them is different. Indian Railways issues train tickets in three categories: confirmed tickets, RAC tickets (reservation against cancellation), and waiting list tickets. Reservation of seats follows a pre-set algorithm that first issues confirmed tickets, followed by RAC tickets, and then waiting list tickets. Now, the question is: Why is it so? The reason behind issuing extra tickets is to utilise the full seating capacity of the train and avoid empty berths due to last-minute cancellations. A typical Indian train carries 1200–1500 passengers in a single run, which means the cancellation of 150–200 tickets for various reasons is normal. To cater to the cancellations, RAC and waiting list tickets are issued. In fact, the railrways introduced current quota reservations to solve a similar situation. It opens after the first chart preparation to fill the remaining seats, if any are available. Coming to the point where you might think that the railrways is issuing waiting list tickets to earn only. Few months back, I travelled by the 12533 Lucknow-Mumbai CSMT Pushpak Express. This train runs with five sleeper coaches, but the railway issues a waiting list of over 200, which surely sounds more than enough as in a normal senario five coaches may have 40–60 cancellations max. After searching a bit, I found that this train had 11–12 sleeper coaches when it was running with ICF rake. After the upgrade, the number of sleeper coaches has been reduced to 5, but the quota is still the same, resulting in a massive crowd in this train. Do share few more such trains where you think that the railways is issuing more waiting list tickets than required. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️. Thank you for your valuable time.

Question: Why has Indian Railways not been privatized yet, even though it has been losing huge amounts of money for many years now?
Answer: Will you invest in a loss making business? I don’t think so. A few years back, Indian Railways came up with an offer for the companies to bid for running trains in India. Initially, the Railways decided to set a base working model for the companies by allowing IRCTC to operate the 1st Corporate Train of India, the "New Delhi-Lucknow Tejas Express.” IRCTC did its best to market the train before its launch, and I must say they were successful. The first corporate train was launched with full zeal and enthusiasm, but how long can you run a train on marketing? Ultimately, you have to justify the fare. Lucknow Tejas was launched with a dynamic fare with no cap, which means the fare will keep on increasing with the demand until a chart is prepared. It means that passengers end up paying 3–4 times the base fare of Shatabdi Express. Tejas was launched with an unique scheme as well in which IRCTC promised to pay a compensatory amount of ₹ 100 if a train gets delayed for more than 1 hour and If it gets late by three hours, you will receive ₹ 250 per person but the timings were set in such a way that getting delayed in a normal scenario was nearly impossible. A slag time of 1 hour was given to the train to be on the safe side. Also, IRCTC already clarified that no compensation amount will be given if a train gets delayed due to fog as it is an "act of God". Additionally, as time passed, the quality of the meal decreased. IRCTC launched two more trains: the Mumbai-Ahmedabad Tejas, which is quite popular, and the Kashi Mahakal Express between Varanasi and Indore, which has been converted into a normal superfast train now, and IRCTC stepped back from its operations. Mumbai-Ahmedabad Tejas was a good example of a corporate train, but Railways built competition by launching Vande Bharat on the same route with no dynamic fare. Overall, we had 3 corporate trains in the last 4 years, two of which are still operational but at a loss. Looking at the condition of corporate trains, it seems like India is not ready for such a model yet, and the railways has realised that too. For now, the Railways is focused on Vande Bharat trains, which are the game changer for the Railways. Failure of the existing working model of corporate trains and priority focus on Vande Bharat trains are two main reasons. However, if we talk about the privatisation of railway stations, then Railways is still working on it. We have two stations privatised so far, whose maintenance is under the control of private companies.100s of railway stations are under modernization, which will be handed over to private companies. Important point: The Indian Railways has already made it clear that train operations will never be privatised. Do share your opinion on this topic in the comment section. Let’s deep dive into the sources one by one: 1 .Earnings from Freight segment: Indian Railways earns its maximum percentage from Freight Segment. To maximise the earnings, IR is also developing a dedicated Corridor “ DFC” for its freight trains. It is expected to be completed by mid 2023. Freight segment contributes almost 50–60% in the total revenue. 2. Earnings from IRCTC: Indian Railways Catering & Tourism Corporation is the subsidary of Indian Railways which handles the department of online ticketing, distributing agent licenses, catering services, tourism, private trains, packed water & much more. Railways holds 87.40% ownership in IRCTC. 3. Earnings from fines/penalities: A lot of passengers still travel with either invalid ticket or without ticket which makes them to pay a fine of ₹250 along with the fare. According to the data published for FY 2019- 20, More than 1 crore passengers were fined for travelling without ticket from which Railways earned a massive amount of 561.73 crores which is 0.26% of total revenue of FY 2019- 20. 4. Earnings from Advertisement and other incomes like e- auction etc.: This segment contributes 0.5- 1 % in the total revenue of Indian Railways. THese were the major source of income for Indian Railways over last few years. Railways is making money through fine paid by the passengers but there is no fine for missing the train or late boarding. Hope this will help you. -Prashant Tiwari ✍️. Question: What is the auto upgradation feature shown while booking a train ticket?
Answer: If you often book your train tickets online then you have surely seen an option named Auto Upgradation on the booking page. I'll try to go into detail about this feature and also discuss its purpose. What is auto upgradation? Auto upgradation is a complementary feature offered by railways to all its passengers, which upgrades their ticket to the higher class if seats are available after the first chart is prepared. How does it work? Suppose you have booked a confirmed train ticket in 3AC and opted for auto upgradation. Now at the time of charting the system checked and found that there is a waiting list in 3 AC but there are 3 seats available in 2AC. In that case, the system will upgrade your ticket to 2AC and vacate a berth for RAC passengers of 3AC and allot RAC to the waiting list passengers. Isn't that cool, right? How is it beneficial for Railways? We all know that online waiting list tickets get canceled after first charting i.e., 4 hours prior to the train's departure time and IRCTC initiates the refund in 1-3 working days. With this feature, the system upgrades a few tickets to higher class and make some seats available in the class where demand is high and allot those seats to RAC passengers whereas Waiting list passengers get RAC and now they can travel. This way Railways reduces the cancellations and of course some amount which they had to refund in case of cancellations. You can opt for an auto upgradation feature for free while booking your train tickets through Trainman. Question: Why is Rajendra Nagar Terminal of Patna called a terminal and trains go two way unlike other terminal stations where trains only go one way?
Answer: This is an interesting question. Before we begin, let's first understand the definition of a terminal railway station. Terminal refers to termination. In context of railways, it is the place where incoming track terminates and does not go further. Coming back to your question, In early 2000s, Rajendra Nagar was a halt station and Patna Junction was serving as the major railway station of Patna. Considering the increase in traffic and daily footfall, the railways decided to develop an alternate station to decrease the load of Patna Junction. Rajendra Nagar was chosen as alternate station & most of the trains originating/terminating from/at Patna were transferred to Rajendra Nagar. The station was given the name Rajendra Nagar Terminal since it was the termination point for many trains coming from Delhi and Kolkata. Question: Is it safe to travel in sleeper coaches of Indian Railways at night time, especially for women travelers alone? What precautions should be taken while travelling on these coaches at night time?
Answer: Travelling in a non-ac sleeper class of Indian railways brings some challenges especially for solo travellers. Passenger’s safety is not a concern but there are some precautions which can be taken during a solo travel in non-ac sleeper class: 1. Always opt for a upper berth especially when it is an overnight journey. Why? Upper berth is considered as most undisturbed berth. You can simply sleep whenever you want and no one will disturb you during the journey. Upper berth is also safer than other berths for small bags like laptop bags, office bags , purse etc. as reaching there is not that convinient & quick. 2. If you are a female traveller then always go for popular trains or trains with lesser stops. Why? Popular trains are generally full and have onboard policemen who ensure the safety & security of passengers & luggage. I know this doesn’t mean100% safety but definitely increase the chances. Trains with lesser stops do not cause heavy movement of passengers in the coach and reduces the chance of theft. 3. Do not carry too many small bags Why? Theft of a small bag is much easier than theft of a heavy trolly bag as it becomes easy in running with a small bag and thieves always look for such bags. You can also put lock on your trolly bags & small bags if possible. 4. Do not use expensive devices like tablets & laptops at railway station. Thieves generally target their hunt at railway stations and using such devices will attract them and you can be their next hunt during journey. 5. Leave your berth only when train is moving at a good speed. Why? Majority of the thefts are reported when train is waiting at outer signal or moving slowly. In a fast moving train thieves can not jump out of the train if cought so they generally avoid. You can also inform your co-passrnger to kerp an eye on your belongings whenever you are going to washroom. 6. Do not leave your phone on berth. Why? Whenever you leave your berth for anything, always keep your phone with you as they are always at first target and also phone is something which can help you in any bad situation. These are the few major points which you can keep in mind during your next solo train journey. Do share your views in the comment section. Question: How has technology streamlined the Indian train travel industry?
Answer: Technology has always replaced the old methods of working over the years. Like others, Indian Railways has also adopted the new technologies over the years which definitely made the working faster, easier & more efficient. There are so many technologies which railways has adopted in terms of safety, signalling, operations, ticketing etc. Today I would like to highlight 3 such technologies which really changed the game for Indian Railways: 1 . HOG Technology We all have seen noisy generator cars at both the ends of almost all LHB trains. Their work was to provide power supply to all the coaches mainly for ac. The technology is known as EOG ( End On Generation) which is now replaced by HOG ( Head On Generation) . So, How this new technology has changed the game? Purpose of HOG is the same as of EOG but the source of power has been changed. Earlier EOG use to generate power through diesel generator installed in the car which was not just costly but also too noisy. Now, HOG simply takes the power from Over head wire and steps down the voltage through transformer installed in the locomotive and then supplies to all the coaches through attachable/detachable cable. 2. KAVACH ( Anti collision system) Indian railways has recently adopted the new generation protection system which simply provides a safety for head to head collisions. In the history, IR has seen few head to head train collisions for example- Gaisal train accident. Such accidents costs alot in terms of people’s life. This technology will stop both the trains automatically well before if they are running on a same track towards each other. 3. Services like Online ticket booking, live running status, Rail madad etc. Few years back, we all use to run towards our nearest railway station to book a ticket or to cancel it. It wasn’t easy at all . Now booking e-tickets has become way easier. You can book your train ticket in some clicks while sitting in your room. Live running status is available for last 6–7 years or even more but it wasn’t that accurate. Earlier it use to provide information with a delay of 10–15 mins. With the new GPS in the Loco technology, we get real time live running status of any train and leave our home for station accordingly. Rail madad is a portal operated by Indian railways to provide a quick support in a running train. We often face problems like cleanliness, theft, water shortage, ac failure, safety and many more. Earlier it wasn’t that easy to file your complaint officially. With Rail Madad you can simply provide some basic deatils with your complaint and any official who is responsible mostly TTE will reach to you with in 20 mins. Isn’t it cool? Question: Why do many important railway junctions have no gravel ballast in the platform area?
Answer: Everything in Indian Railways is for a reason and here too, there is a reason. We often find cemented rail beds at major railway stations whereas normal ballast rail beds are used for other stations and route. The reason for using a cemented rail bed is very simple, i.e., cleanliness. With cemented rail beds, it becomes easier for staff to maintain cleanliness at major stations. A few years back, there were no bio toilets, and all human waste was discharged onto the tracks. We all know that trains at major stations stop for 10–20 minutes, which means more waste on the tracks. The railways came up with this idea to maintain cleanliness at major stations, and it really worked. Nowadays, trains have bio-toilets, so no human waste goes on tracks. Sometimes people leave some wrappers, used disposals, etc. which are cleaned by staff. Do share your views in the comment section and points if I missed them here. Question: How will loco pilots know that they are arriving on any station?
Answer: There are few things through which loco pilots can easily know that they are approaching to any station. 1 . When a loco pilot starts his/her duty, they are provided with all the details of the route to which they are going. This includes each and every thing. All station with kilomettes, curves, speed limits, bridges, tunnels etc. You might think that how they are informed the exact location of any bridge or tunnel or any speed limit. In that case kilo mettes stones/ pole numbers are used. For example: If there is a speed limit between two stations then it will be mentioned that from poles no. 125/3 to 130/5 speed will be 20 kmph. Here, 125 & 130 is the kilomettes from any major station of that route. 3 & 5 is the pole no. falling in that particular kilometer. Usually there are 18 to 20 poles in one kilometre distance. With the pole number loco pilots can also know the approaching station. 2. With the help of Approaching signal. Every station has approach signal and this is the clear sign that you are approaching to a station. Signals can be seen from more than a kilometer if there is no curve. Question: What are the ways to join Indian Railways as an ALP/LP?
Answer: Getting a job in the railways is a dream of many people and it is a matter of pride for ourselves to be part of Indian Railways whose network is spread all over the country. The post of an Assistant Loco pilot is one of the most responsible post in Indian Railways. Recruitment conducted by RRBs on this post is done in two ways: 1. Direct Recruitment through RRB exam 2. Departmental promotion through GDCE(General Departmental competitive exam). To become an Assistant Loco Pilot (ALP), a candidate needs to have qualified matriculation or equivalent qualification from a recognized board plus the Candidate must have completed Act Apprentice or ITI pass or Diploma or Degree(Btech) in Mechanical/Electrical/Electronics/Automobile Engineering from an institution recognized by AICTE. A candidate’s age must fall into the range of 18 years to 28 years. The reserved category (SC/ST/OBC/EWS/PWD/ExSM) candidates get relaxation in upper age limit according to the rules laid down by the Government. Selection Process The selection of candidates for Assistant Loco Pilot posts is done on the basis of their performance in the Computer based tests. First Stage Computer Based Test (CBT 1), Second Stage Computer Based Test (CBT 2), Computer Based Aptitude Test (CBAT) and Document Verification. CBT1 is conducted for 60 minute duration and consists of 75 questions while the CBT2 consists of 150 questions in two parts – Part A and Part B. Part A is of 90 minute duration and consists of 100 questions while Part B is of 60 minute duration and consists of 75 questions. There is negative marking of 1/3 in CBT at both the stages. The candidates who qualify both the rounds (CBT1 & CBT2) are called for Computer Based Aptitude Test (CBAT) and after qualifying the candidates are called for document verification. All the candidates who qualify all the above parameters in merit they will be called for Medical test. Mind you, ALP falls under safety category hence a strict health checking is done in which both eyes must be 6/6 without any refractive surgery. Glasses also not allowed. Body should not have any other deformation or medical condition. After working for several years, Assistant Loco Pilot is promoted to the Senior Assistant Loco Pilot post and then promoted to Loco Pilot level. You can also apply for other departmental exam as ALP & LP both. Note: You can not become a Loco pilot directly. Image source: google Thank you for reading the answer.

Question: Why are they using three banker locomotives instead of one or two locomotive at the Bhor Ghat section?
Answer: Bankers are used to support the couplings of the train when it moves to an elevated section. Bankers also support to the primary locomotive in climbing with a train. When a train climbs , load on the first coupling which joins Primary locomotive to all the other coaches is highest which increases the risk of coupling breakdown. To avoid this breakdown, Banker locomotives are used. ( Circuled part is the part of the coupling which usually breaks) Why three banker locomotives are used? A 10 coach train can easily climb with one banker and one primary locomotive , a 24 coach train needs two banker locomotives as the load increases and a 60 wagon loaded freight train needs at least three banker locomotives. It obviously takes time to attach and dettach the banker locomotives from the train but if they have to couple amd decouple between the banker locomotives again and again as per the train then the time will increase by some 20 mins. more. To avoid this unnecessary delay a set of three banker locomotives is used for all type of trains. Image source: google Thank you for reading the answer.

Question: Why don’t loco pilots increase the speed of the train and drive fast when the train is already delayed to reach its destination?

Travelling time of any two station is fixed as per the max permissible speed. For example, If distance between station A to B is 10 kms and max permissible speed is 60 kmph then the train has to cover this distance in 10 mins. or more and if the train is covering this distance in less than 10 mins regularly on all stations then the control will inform to the concern department and the case of over speeding will be filed on locopilots & guard. Guard is responsible for the speed also and he/she can ask locopilot to slow down if he/she finds the over speeding. Hope provided information will help you. Question: When the signal remains clear in front of the train, why does the station master show the flag?
Answer: Green signal indicates the route clearance but Green flag shown by the Station Master and anyone from the staff ( on the other side) has its own significance. 1 . Green flag from the loco pilot and assistant loco pilot to station master signals that all controls in the train are working properly and the section they just cleared is safe for other trains. Note: Pilot and assistant loco pilot keeps an eye on UP/DOWN line all the time and reports to the next station master if they find anything unusual. 2. Green flag from station master and staff to the locopilots signals that everything is clear at zero point. Note: It is the rule in the railways that once any through train gets a green signal then the station master will not change it in red. He/She will show a red flag if he/she finds anything unusual. This is done to avoid derailment in case of emergency braking. 3. Green flag shown to guard by station master signals that everything is ok in the train( which includes axle heat, fire and any smoke) and signals from the passengers. In case of emergency , if passengers are not able to stop the train by pulling the chain then they will show some red cloth or some indications which can be noticed by station master only and he/she can either show a red flag to guard or immediately report to next station and control. 4. Green flag waved by guard, locopilots and station master signals that they have acknowledged their signals. Question: What are axle counters in railways, and how do they work for safe operations of trains?
Answer: An axle counter is a device that detects the passing of a train between two points on a track. A counting head (or detection point) is installed at each end of the section, and as each train axle passes the counting head at the start of the section, a detection point comprises two independent sensors, therefore the device can detect the direction and speed of a train by the order and time in which the sensors are passed. As the train passes a similar counting head at the end of the section, the counter compares count at the end of the section with that recorded at the beginning. If the two counts are the same, the section is presumed to be clear for a second train. Advantages The advantages of Axle counter that- ●An axle counter system can cover a very long section up to 15 Kms. ●It does not get affected either by flooding of track or poor maintenance of tracks unlike the track circuit, which is highly susceptible to these conditions. ●It does not require insulating rail joints, thus, rails can be continuously welded. This reduces track maintenance cost, low wear and tear of tracks and vehicles and to increase traveling comfort. ●Efficiency and safe working of axle counters does not depend up various track parameters and climate condition such as length, ballast condition, drainage, stray voltage and currents, track feed voltage and lead cables, etc. like track circuits. Disadvantages ●The quality of the electrical signal transmitted by the rail is dependent on the insulation resistance of the ties and the ballast. Causes leakage currents (if insufficient). ●This resistance is a limiting factor for the maximum length of the track circuit. Applications Axle counters have been finding more and more uses on modern safety signaling systems in railways. These are being used presently for the following. •Monitoring of berthing tracks in station areas and yards. •Monitoring of point zones in station areas and yard. •Automatic Signaling systems. •Block working through axle counters using multiplexers (USBI) with cable, OFC or radio communication (Last Vehicle Checking Device /Axle Counter Block Working/Block Proving by Axle Counter). •Level-crossing warning system using axle counter. (f) Intermediate Block Signaling in Double line sections. Note: If the axle couts at the start of the section/station or block and at the end of the section are not same then the section will not be cleared for the next train. This removes the chances of collision of two trains. Sources: Fersil, systèmes sécuritaires ferroviaires | Fersil; Wikipedia; Central Electronics Limited-Universal ; google images. Question: What are loco sheds in railways?
Answer: Locomotive sheds are meant for the maintenance and servicing of locomotives. The location and design of a locomotive shed depends on the volume and pattern of traffic, the layout of the terminal station and the marshalling yard, and other allied factors. Locomotive sheds are normally spaced at about 250 to 300 km apart in order to avoid the idle movement of locomotives and crew. Locomotive sheds are basically of two types. Homing sheds: These are provided to house locomotives and attend to their maintenance and servicing. Equal stress is laid on the servicing and maintenance of locomotives in these sheds. These sheds are normally designed to house about 80 to 100 locomotives. Turn round sheds: These are provided for servicing locomotives and bringing them back to the homing sheds. They may also be provided for attending to certain minor repairs. These sheds are normally designed to hold about 30 to 50 locomotives. How can one tell which home shed a loco belongs to? Home sheds for locos are often, but not always, indicated somewhere on the loco itself. For instance, the station code of the home shed may be painted on the side of the loco, or the full name of the shed may appear on the front. Some sheds have elaborate logos, whereas others may just bear stylized renditions of the shed names. Logos often appear on the front, but are sometimes on the sides of locos (e.g., Erode, Lallaguda, Vadodara). Some sheds don't use any logos, e.g., Santragachhi, Mughalsarai. Station codes often appear near the buffers on one side. For many sheds (e.g., Howrah, Kanpur, Mughalsarai) the shed station code appears in Roman letters on one side and the full name of the shed in Devanagari on the other. Question: How does the interlocking system work in Indian Railways, and how does it ensure the safety of passengers?
Answer: Interlocking means an arrangement of signals, poonts( track change) and other appliances, operated from a panel or lever frame to insure the safe operation of trains. ( Route Relay Interlocking) Points, signals and other units are usually operated by means of levers, interconnecting between these levers is accomplished either by mechanical or by electrical means. At less important stations the point, signals and other levers are interlocked by means of keys which are used of lock or release the levers, either in the normal or in the reverse position, as required. ( manual interlocking) At other stations, the levers are interlocked by means of tappets inside a box of the lever frame, which is normally kept covered and sealed. Electrically operated interlocking In the more advanced electrical or electronic interlocking schemes, the points and signals are worked from one integrated mechanism in a signal cabin which features a display of the entire track layout with indications of sections that are occupied, free, set for reception or dispatch, etc. There are two types of electrical interlocking: 1 . Panel Interlocking (PI) is the system used in most medium-sized stations on IR. In this, the points and signals are worked by individual switches that control them. ( Panel Interlocking) 2. Route Relay Interlocking (RRI) is the system used in large and busy stations that have to handle high volumes of train movements. In this, an entire route through the station can be selected and all the associated points and signals along the route can be set at once by a switch for receiving, holding, blocking, or dispatching trains. As an example, Old Delhi station has an RRI system from Siemens which allows selection from among 1122 possible routes. CR has a large RRI system at Kurla which controls signals from Ghatkopar to Sion on the Main Line, at Lokmanya Tilak Terminus, and from Chembur to GTB Nagar on the Harbour Line. The first route-relay interlocking system was set up on WR at Churchgate station control tower in the 1950s . RRI and PI equipment is from Siemens and some British manufacturers. In recent years interlocking accomplished by modern integrated electronic circuitry instead of electromechanical relay systtems has come into use (Solid State Interlocking ('SSI'). SSI is in place at 14 stations in India. SSI equipment is manufactured by RDSO. 247+ stations have RRI installations, and 2,426+ have Panel Interlocking. ( Solid State Interlocking) Image source: Google Thank you for reading the answer.

Question: What are the MEMU EMU DMU trains? How does it work?
Answer: We all know that most of the trains are pulled by locomotive (engine), but in multiple unit sets like EMU/MEMU, multiple coaches are powered. It means that in ordinary train, only locomotive (engine) has a traction motor attached to it for running whole train. But in multiple unit trains, coaches are self propelled or you can say that coaches do not need any locomotive. All powered coaches are connected thorough MU (multiple unit) cable and all the motors of powered coaches are controlled by controller or motor man from any of the two ends. DEMU( Diesel Electric Multiple Unit) , it works on the same principle as the diesel locomotives. Diesel genetator of 750 HP produces electricity which is fed to the traction motors of the power car and also in the trailer car having traction motor. Usually traction motors are provided at both ends of the rake. A new aerodynamic design of DEMU introduced in 2004 on the SCR. It consists of 8 car rakes (Two motor car and six Trailer cars ). ELECTRICAL MULTIPLE UNIT EMU are preffered for suburban section as it have high accerleration and phenomenal stopping distances allowing them to achieve higher speed at a short time and stopping efficiently hence it ultimately offers high throughput. Mainly two different emu's are in use , these are: • 1.5 KV DC traction • 25 KV AC traction MEMU's known as Main Line EMU. It was first introduced in 1993 by ICF so that it can be operated in more areas. Unlike the EMU's they have vestibule connection (gangway connection) and lavatories. Question: Which is the most delayed train of Indian Railways?

Making matters worse, According to The Economic Times, on time performance of trains has dipped further to 65 per cent in the past three months. The report added that currently several long-route trains are running up to 20 hours late, causing massive inconvenience to the millions of people travelling on the world's busiest public transportation network daily. The premier Champaran Humsafar train, launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi to celebrate 100 years of Mahatma Gandhi's Champaran Satyagraha in April 2018, on average runs 12 hours behind schedule. Question: What is the difference between an i-ticket and an e-ticket in India's online train ticket?
Answer: When we book online train tickets in India through www.irctc.co.in, we have two options called: Type: i-ticket or e-ticket, out of which we have to select one. The nomenclature is confusing but here's the difference: 1. iTicket - It is the fancy name for a paper ticket bought through IRCTC’s website. You specify the journey details, passenger information, and pay online. The ticket is sent through courier to the delivery address specified. This is the same as the ticket you get when you buy from a railway booking counter. Downside: A. You cannot cancel this ticket online. You have to queue up at a railway booking counter and produce the ticket and the booking clerk cancels it for you. B. You have to buy an iTicket at least 3 days before the journey date. This time is required because the ticket is physically delivered to the customer's address.  2. eTicket - Stands for 'electronic ticket'. It's a paperless, online-only ticket. The ticket is delivered to you in the form of an email that you can print. The railway authorities also sms your ticket. You simply need to show either the sms or a printout of the email to the TTE. The main theme is to save trees so go paperless and save environment.You can cancel the ticket online and It can be booked upto 30 minutes before the departure of the train from last charting station. Hope, This will help you. Thank you for reading the answer.

Question: What is your favorite rail route in India and why?
Answer: Many of us who love travelling in railways also love this route and those who don’t will definitly think of travelling at least once on this route after reading this answer. Yes, I am talking about Mumbai -Manglore route ( Konkan Railways). Designed and built by Indian engineers in a record time of eight years, the Konkan Railway takes you on a breathtaking journey through rugged mountains, lush valleys, sunlit paddy fields, bustling villages and glistening rivers that lead out to sea, the construction of Konkan Railway effectively connected the southwestern coast of India with the rest of the country in a point-to-point straight line. It is undoubtedly one of the biggest and most difficult infrastructure projects India has undertaken and successfully completed since Independence. Today, the Konkan Railway travels 738 kilometers through the states of Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka, starting just after the Roha railway station (75 km south of Panvel in the suburbs of Mumbai) in Maharashtra and ending at the Thokur railway station near Mangalore in southern Karnataka. This scenic route has around 2000 big and small bridges, 92 tunnels and India’s then-longest ever tunnel at Karbude, which is 6.5 km. in length. The route also has a 424 viaduct for a single line of broad gauge track over the Panval river. It connects two hills and has 12 spans and 10 pillars, 6 of which are taller than the Qutub Minar ! At present, it is the third highest viaduct in Asia. The Konkan Railway is an Indian triumph in many areas – engineering, efficiency, innovation, and dedication. Even today, a journey on this spectacular route, with its resplendent views of the Western Ghats, is an experience that remains etched in your memory for a long, long time. Best season to experience the beauty of this route is monsoon. Caution : Do not continuously watch the tunnels. It may result in dizziness. Question: What are the pros and cons of Indian Railways introducing biometric entry in general coaches of trains?
Answer: Let me first tell you how this system works. This passenger friendly step is taken for the general class passengers to reduce the rush and stampede like situation at platforms at the time of boarding trains with unreserved coaches(pros). The additional benefit of the initiative is that it does away with corrupt practices in allocation of seats and also helps the Railway Protection Force (RPF) identify possible thieves through fingerprint records. How does new biometric system for unreserved coaches work? Passengers purchasing tickets for the general class coaches will have to get their fingerprints scanned at the biometric machine, after which a token will be generated. The total number of tokens generated will be in line with the number of seats in a particular general class coach. The passengers can then assemble in a queue as per their serial number on the token a few minutes before the rake is placed on the platform. The RPF staff at the entry point of the general class coach verifies the token serial number and allows the passengers to board the coach in an orderly manner. Indian Railways has procured 4 biometric machines, 2 each for the Mumbai Central railway station and Bandra Terminus station. The biometric machine is being used for the general class coaches of the following trains: ●Amravati Express (Mumbai Central station) ●Jaipur Superfast Express (Mumbai Central station) ●Karnavati Express (Mumbai Central station) ●Gujarat Mail (Mumbai Central station) ●Golden Temple Mail (Mumbai Central station) ●Paschim Express (Bandra Terminus) ●Amaravati Express (Bandra Terminus) ●Avadh Express (Bandra Terminus) ●Maharashtra Sampark Kranti Express (Bandra Terminus). Cons All is good but what about other stations where above mentioned trains will hault? This system can manage passengers at the originating station but later the situation of the coaches will be same as it is not installed on others stations yet . If Railway installs such machines on all major station as soon as possible then we will be able to find the real impact of this system in the condition of general coaches.
